Higher-order networks: three readings of one dataset

honets

2026-08-26

Each section below is one verb, worked end to end on the same data. The sections run in order in a single R session, so later ones may reuse objects the earlier ones built.

Three higher-order readings of one dataset

The analytic question

“Higher-order network” names three different objects in the literature, and they are usually treated as three literatures. A network is higher-order when a relation reaches past a single pair of nodes at a single moment — but there are two distinct ways to reach past it, and three structures that do so:

  • a relation can depend on more than the current node — a memory network;
  • a relation can bind more than two nodes at once, either as a set whose every subset is also a relation — a simplicial complex — or as a set with no such requirement — a hypergraph.

This tutorial puts all three on the same data and asks a question that only a single package can ask cleanly: do they agree? If they did, the choice among them would be a matter of taste. They do not, and where they disagree is the finding.

The data are human_long, bundled with honets: 10,796 coded human turns from 429 human-AI pair-programming sessions, nine action codes.

library(honets)
library(cograph)

The baseline says nothing

Before reaching for any higher-order structure, run the first-order one. It is the model that must be beaten.

fo <- build_hon(human_long, action = "code", actor = "session_id",
                time = "timestamp", max_order = 1, min_freq = 5)
hon_centrality(fo)
      state  pagerank betweenness closeness
1   Command 0.1111111           0         8
2   Correct 0.1111111           0         8
3 Frustrate 0.1111111           0         8
4   Inquire 0.1111111           0         8
5 Interrupt 0.1111111           0         8
6    Refine 0.1111111           0         8
7   Request 0.1111111           0         8
8   Specify 0.1111111           0         8
9    Verify 0.1111111           0         8

Every action gets PageRank exactly 1/9, closeness exactly 8, betweenness exactly 0. That is not a numerical coincidence. With 10,796 turns over nine codes, every one of the 81 possible transitions occurs at least five times, so the first-order network is the complete digraph on nine nodes. Every node has the same in-degree, which forces PageRank uniform; every pair is one step apart, which forces closeness constant and betweenness zero.

The first-order network is structurally incapable of ranking these actions. No choice of centrality repairs that — the information is not in the topology. Everything below is an attempt to put it back.

Reading 1 — memory: what follows what, given how you got here

A memory network makes a node a state plus the memory of how it was reached, so Specify -> Command is a different object from Inquire -> Command, with its own continuation distribution.

hon <- build_hon(human_long, action = "code", actor = "session_id",
                 time = "timestamp", max_order = 3, min_freq = 5)
hon
Higher-Order Network (HON)
  Nodes:        233 (9 first-order states)
  Edges:        819
  Max order:    3 (requested 3)
  Min freq:     5
  Trajectories: 425
hon_centrality(hon, type = "pagerank", sort_by = "pagerank")
      state   pagerank
1   Specify 0.23396968
2   Command 0.18365067
3   Inquire 0.10991607
4 Frustrate 0.10421334
5   Request 0.09503177
6    Refine 0.08850329
7   Correct 0.07833723
8 Interrupt 0.06438203
9    Verify 0.04199591

Nine states, but 233 nodes: the extra 224 are memory contexts. And now the actions separate over a 5.6-fold range — Specify holds 23.4% of the flow, Command 18.4%, down to Verify at 4.2%.

This is a claim about flow: where a walker that respects the sequences’ memory spends its time.

The memory reading, drawn. The object to draw is fo, the first-order network from the opening section — nine states. The higher-order network has 233 nodes and drawing it produces a hairball, so the memory structure goes on top of the nine-node layout as pathways rather than becoming the layout.

splot(fo, minimum = 0.05, title = "Reading 1 - the nine states")

contexts_top <- as.data.frame(hon, order_min = 2, sort_by = "count", top = 6)
plot_simplicial(fo,
                pathways = contexts_top,
                max_pathways = 6,
                title = "Reading 1 - memory, as pathways")

Reading 2 — simplicial: which actions co-occur as coherent groups

The same fitted memory network can be read as a pathway complex: every observed path becomes a simplex, and — this is what makes it simplicial — so does every sub-path of it. That closure is what gives the object a geometry.

sc <- build_simplicial(hon, type = "pathway")
sc
Pathway Complex 
  9 nodes, 157 simplices, dimension 3
  Density: 61.6%  |  Mean dim: 1.87  |  Euler: 19
  f-vector: (f0=9 f1=36 f2=79 f3=33)
  Betti: b0=1 b2=18
  Nodes: Command, Correct, Frustrate, Inquire, Interrupt, Refine, Request, Specify, Verify 
as.data.frame(sc, what = "f_vector")
  dim count
1   0     9
2   1    36
3   2    79
4   3    33

Nine nodes carry 157 simplices up to dimension 3: 36 edges, 79 triangles, 33 tetrahedra. Density 61.6% — most of the combinations that could appear do.

Because it has a geometry, it has a topology:

betti_numbers(sc)
b0 b1 b2 b3 
 1  0 18  0 
euler_characteristic(sc)
[1] 19

b0 = 1 says the complex is connected — no group of actions is isolated from the rest. b1 = 0 says there are no one-dimensional holes: any loop of actions can be filled in by observed pathways. b2 = 18 says there are 18 independent two-dimensional voids — configurations of four actions where every triple was observed but the four-way combination never was. Those are the near-misses of this corpus: patterns the sessions came right up to the edge of and never completed.

Per-action, the simplicial reading is a count of memberships:

simplicial_degree(sc)
       node d0 d1 d2 d3 total
8   Specify  1  8 28 32    68
1   Command  1  8 28 19    55
7   Request  1  8 26 15    49
2   Correct  1  8 26 12    46
3 Frustrate  1  8 26 12    46
4   Inquire  1  8 25 13    46
6    Refine  1  8 27 11    46
5 Interrupt  1  8 26 10    44
9    Verify  1  8 25  8    41

Specify sits in 68 simplices, Verify in 41. Note the shape of the table: d0/d1 are identical for every action (each is in one vertex and eight edges — a consequence of the saturated first-order structure), so the whole signal is in d2 and d3. The discrimination lives entirely in the three- and four-way combinations.

The simplicial reading, drawn. This one has its own plot() method, and it is the right picture: face counts by dimension, the Betti numbers, and each action’s simplicial degree. The blob diagram above showed which pathways; this shows the shape they add up to.

plot(sc)

Reading 3 — hypergraph: which actions belong to the same session

A hypergraph drops the closure requirement: a set of nodes can be a relation without any of its subsets being one. That fits observed group membership exactly. Each session is one hyperedge over the codes it contains.

hg <- group_hypergraph(human_long, actor = "code", group = "session_id")
hg
Hypergraph: 9 nodes, 429 hyperedges
Size distribution:
  size_1   : 5
  size_2   : 3
  size_3   : 20
  size_4   : 32
  size_5   : 62
  size_6   : 77
  size_7   : 75
  size_8   : 75
  size_9   : 80
Source: group membership (member = code, group = session_id)
measures <- hypergraph_measures(hg)
as.data.frame(measures, what = "global")
                 measure       value
1                n_nodes   9.0000000
2           n_hyperedges 429.0000000
3                density   0.7293447
4          avg_edge_size   6.5641026
5 pairwise_participation   1.0000000

429 hyperedges — one per session — averaging 6.6 actions each. The distribution is heavily weighted toward large sessions: 80 of the 429 sessions use all nine codes.

hypergraph_centrality(hg, type = "pagerank", sort_by = "pagerank")
       node   pagerank
1   Command 0.14396265
2   Specify 0.14158683
3 Interrupt 0.13500987
4   Request 0.12297636
5   Correct 0.09773453
6   Inquire 0.09562551
7 Frustrate 0.09298612
8    Refine 0.08727062
9    Verify 0.08284752

This is a claim about co-membership: how much of a random walk that hops action → session → action lands on each action.

The hypergraph reading, drawn. A hypergraph has no direct network picture, so it goes through clique_expansion() — and the caption has to say so, because the projection is a lossy one.

net <- clique_expansion(hg)
splot(net, minimum = 0.05,
      title = "Reading 3 - hypergraph, projected")

Three pictures of the same 10,796 turns. The first is directed and carries memory; the second is undirected and carries closure; the third is undirected, complete, and carries only co-membership weight. Nothing about the data changed — only the question.

Do the three agree?

Three tidy tables, joined in two steps. Nothing here reaches into a result object.

pr_memory <- hon_centrality(hon, type = "pagerank")
deg_simplicial <- simplicial_degree(sc)
pr_hypergraph <- hypergraph_centrality(hg, type = "pagerank")
cmp <- merge(pr_memory, deg_simplicial, by.x = "state", by.y = "node")
cmp <- merge(cmp, pr_hypergraph, by.x = "state", by.y = "node",
             suffixes = c("_memory", "_hypergraph"))
cmp
      state pagerank_memory d0 d1 d2 d3 total pagerank_hypergraph
1   Command      0.18365067  1  8 28 19    55          0.14396265
2   Correct      0.07833723  1  8 26 12    46          0.09773453
3 Frustrate      0.10421334  1  8 26 12    46          0.09298612
4   Inquire      0.10991607  1  8 25 13    46          0.09562551
5 Interrupt      0.06438203  1  8 26 10    44          0.13500987
6    Refine      0.08850329  1  8 27 11    46          0.08727062
7   Request      0.09503177  1  8 26 15    49          0.12297636
8   Specify      0.23396968  1  8 28 32    68          0.14158683
9    Verify      0.04199591  1  8 25  8    41          0.08284752
cmp_ranks <- subset(cmp, select = c(pagerank_memory, total, pagerank_hypergraph))
cor(cmp_ranks, method = "spearman")
                    pagerank_memory     total pagerank_hypergraph
pagerank_memory           1.0000000 0.8703883           0.5500000
total                     0.8703883 1.0000000           0.6789029
pagerank_hypergraph       0.5500000 0.6789029           1.0000000

The memory and simplicial readings agree strongly (Spearman 0.87) — both are built from the same fitted pathways, so this is a consistency check rather than independent evidence. The interesting number is 0.55: memory flow and hypergraph co-membership rank these nine actions differently.

Two actions carry that disagreement, in opposite directions.

Interrupt is 8th of 9 by memory flow (0.064) and 3rd by co-membership (0.135). It appears in 393 of the 429 sessions — third highest hyperdegree — yet the transitions into and out of it are not on heavily travelled paths. Interrupt is ubiquitous but peripheral: almost every session contains one, and almost none is organised around it.

Frustrate runs the other way: 4th by memory flow (0.104), 7th by co-membership (0.093). It shows up in fewer sessions (252) but when it does, it sits on paths the walk keeps returning to. Frustration is localised but consequential.

Neither reading is wrong. They answer different questions, and an analysis that reports only one of them will describe Interrupt as either a central action or a marginal one, with no way to see that both are true.

Crossing back

The families are entry points into one another. A hypergraph projects back to an ordinary pairwise network, which any first-order tool accepts:

net <- clique_expansion(hg)
summary(net)
Cograph Network Summary
======================

Structure:
  Nodes: 9 
  Edges: 36 
  Type: Undirected 

Edge Statistics:
  Min weight: 139 
  Max weight: 410 
  Mean weight: 238.472 

Node Labels:
   Command, Correct, Frustrate, Inquire, Interrupt, Refine, Request, Specify, Verify 

Layout: not computed

Nine nodes, 36 edges — the complete undirected graph, weighted by how often each pair shared a session. Compare that to the first-order network this tutorial opened with: same saturation, but now the weights carry the co-membership information, so the projection is not the degenerate object the transition network was.

Choosing a reading

  • Memory network (build_hon()) — the question is about order and history: what follows what, and does the past matter. Check markov_order_test() first: if memory is not there, the simpler model should be reported.
  • Simplicial complex (build_simplicial()) — the question is about coherent groups and their geometry: which combinations hold together, and what is conspicuously missing. betti_numbers() finds the absences; a first-order summary can only report presences.
  • Hypergraph (group_hypergraph(), window_hypergraph()) — the question is about co-membership: which things belong to the same occasion, with no assumption that sub-groups are meaningful in themselves.
  • All three — when an action’s role is contested. The gap between the readings is the finding, as it is for Interrupt here.

Two cautions. The simplicial reading above was built from the memory network, so its agreement with the memory ranking is partly structural; build it from an independently estimated network if you need the two to be independent evidence. And every number here is a point estimate — use bootstrap_hon() before reporting a memory-based ranking as a finding.

See also

  • Higher-order centrality — the memory family in depth, including which contexts carry the flow.
  • Bootstrap and permutation inference — how stable a rule is under resampling.
  • Windowed sequence hyperedges — the other route from sequences into the hypergraph family.
  • Hypergraph PageRank — edge-dependent vertex weights, and when a hypergraph collapses to a pairwise graph.

References

  • Battiston, F., Cencetti, G., Iacopini, I., Latora, V., Lucas, M., Patania, A., Young, J.-G., & Petri, G. (2020). Networks beyond pairwise interactions: Structure and dynamics. Physics Reports, 874, 1-92.
  • Bianconi, G. (2021). Higher-Order Networks. Cambridge University Press.
  • Scholtes, I., Wider, N., & Garas, A. (2016). Higher-order aggregate networks in the analysis of temporal networks. The European Physical Journal B, 89, 61.
  • Atkin, R. H. (1974). Mathematical Structure in Human Affairs. Heinemann.
  • Chitra, U., & Raphael, B. J. (2019). Random walks on hypergraphs with edge-dependent vertex weights. ICML 2019, PMLR 97, 1172-1181.

pathways(): the bridge between the three families

The analytic question

The three structure families in honets are entry points into one another, not islands. pathways() is the generic that carries a fitted memory network across to the other two: it extracts the paths the model considers real and returns them as plain strings, which build_simplicial(type = "pathway") turns into a complex.

It is a small verb doing one job, and it is the reason a HON can be handed to a topological analysis without any manual reshaping.

library(honets)
seqs <- split(human_long$code, human_long$session_id)
library(cograph)

Three methods, one generic

pathways() dispatches on net_hon, net_hypa and net_mogen. Each returns the paths that model regards as meaningful — which is a different set in each case, because the three models mean different things by “meaningful”.

hon <- build_hon(seqs, max_order = 2, min_freq = 50)
p_hon <- pathways(hon)
length(p_hon)
[1] 25
pathways(hon, top = 6)
[1] "Specify Command -> Specify"   "Command Request -> Specify"  
[3] "Specify Command -> Request"   "Request Specify -> Interrupt"
[5] "Command Command -> Command"   "Command Specify -> Interrupt"

From a HON: the extracted rules — contexts that earned their own node. 25 of them at min_freq = 50.

hp <- build_hypa(seqs, order = 2)
p_hypa <- pathways(hp)
length(p_hypa)

From HYPA: the anomalous paths — those significantly over- or under-represented against the degree-preserving null. 185 of them. Note the first entry, Interrupt Interrupt -> Interrupt: the same repeated- interruption pattern that path_dependence() flags as the highest-divergence context.

mo <- build_mogen(seqs, max_order = 2)
p_mogen <- pathways(mo)
length(p_mogen)
[1] 702
pathways(mo, top = 4)
[1] "Specify Command -> Specify"   "Command Request -> Specify"  
[3] "Specify Command -> Request"   "Request Specify -> Interrupt"

From MOGen: every path in the fitted layer — 702, the complete second-order transition set, because a multi-order model does not prune.

The format

Each string is "<context states, space separated> -> <next state>". The context uses spaces so that the arrow separates history from continuation unambiguously.

p_hon[1]
[1] "Specify Command -> Specify"

Read as: the context Specify Command continuing to Specify.

Crossing to the simplicial family

sc <- build_simplicial(hon, type = "pathway")
sc
Pathway Complex 
  9 nodes, 29 simplices, dimension 2
  Density: 22.5%  |  Mean dim: 0.90  |  Euler: 1
  f-vector: (f0=9 f1=14 f2=6)
  Betti: b0=2 b1=1
  Nodes: Command, Correct, Frustrate, Inquire, Interrupt, Refine, Request, Specify, Verify

build_simplicial() calls pathways() internally — you rarely need to call it yourself. Each path becomes a simplex, and because a simplicial complex is closed under subsets, so does every sub-path. The result has a geometry, and therefore a topology: b0 = 2 says the well-evidenced pathways fall into two disconnected groups of actions, and b1 = 1 says there is one one-dimensional hole — a cycle of actions that is never closed by an observed pathway.

Neither statement is available from the transition network the paths came from.

Seeing them

Whichever model produced them, pathways draw the same way — as blobs over the first-order nine-node layout. The higher-order object supplies the pathways; it is never the thing drawn. Compare the sources by eye: HON gives the contexts that earned a node, HYPA the ones that deviate from the null, MOGen every fitted path.

net1 <- build_hon(seqs, max_order = 1)
contexts_top <- as.data.frame(hon, order_min = 2, sort_by = "count", top = 6)
plot_simplicial(net1,
                pathways = contexts_top,
                max_pathways = 6, title = "Pathways from build_hon()")

plot_simplicial(hp, anomaly = "over", max_pathways = 6,
                dismantled = TRUE, ncol = 3)

The choice of source model matters

Because the three models select different paths, they build different complexes:

do.call(rbind, lapply(
  list(HON = hon, HYPA = hp, MOGen = mo),
  function(m) {
    p <- pathways(m)
    s <- build_simplicial(m, type = "pathway")
    f_vector <- as.data.frame(s, what = "f_vector")
    betti <- betti_numbers(s)
    data.frame(paths = length(p), simplices = sum(f_vector$count),
               dimension = max(f_vector$dim), b0 = betti[["b0"]])
  }))
      paths simplices dimension b0
HON      25        29         2  2
HYPA    185       105         2  1
MOGen   702       129         2  1

MOGen’s 702 unpruned paths produce a dense, connected complex; HON’s 25 well-evidenced rules produce a sparse, disconnected one. The topology you report is a property of the model you chose, not of the raw sequences — say which model, and say why.

Calling it directly

You would call pathways() yourself to inspect what a model considers real, or to feed the paths somewhere else:

# how long are the extracted paths?
table(lengths(strsplit(p_hon, " ", fixed = TRUE)))

 4 
25

What to do next

  • build_simplicial() — the main consumer, and where the topology gets computed.
  • build_hon(), build_hypa(), build_mogen() — the three producers.
  • window_hypergraph() — the other route out of sequence data, into the hypergraph family.
